meta.title: Who really said "Gilding the lily"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare wrote “to gild refined gold, to paint the lily” in King John — never “gild the lily.” The famous idiom is a conflation of his line.
meta.ogDescription: Shakespeare wrote “to paint the lily,” not “gild the lily.” The popular idiom is a documented misquotation of King John.

answer.label: Not Shakespeare’s words — a misquotation of King John
answer.sourceLine: The idea is Shakespeare’s, but the wording is not. In King John (Act 4, Scene 2) Salisbury says it is wasteful excess “To gild refined gold, to paint the lily” — he gilds the gold and paints the lily. The popular idiom “gilding the lily” collapses those two images into one and swaps the verb, a conflation Shakespeare never wrote.

source.heading: The genuine line in King John

docMeta.dd: “to gild refined gold, to paint the lily”

source.excerpt:
Therefore, to be possess’d with double pomp,
To guard a title that was rich before,
To gild refined gold, to paint the lily,
To throw a perfume on the violet,
To smooth the ice, or add another hue
Unto the rainbow, or with taper-light
To seek the beauteous eye of heaven to garnish,
Is wasteful and ridiculous excess.
trail: Shakespeare’s line, spoken by Salisbury in King John, Act 4 Scene 2, is “To gild refined gold, to paint the lily” — he never wrote “gild the lily.”
The Grammarphobia Blog confirms the phrase Shakespeare used was “paint the lily,” and that the “gild the lily” misquotation has become far more common in modern usage.
Wiktionary calls “gild the lily” a common misquotation of the King John line and records Edith Wharton using it in A Motor-Flight Through France (1908).
source.excerptNote: Salisbury’s speech criticising King John’s needless second coronation. Note the two separate images: one gilds refined gold, the other paints the lily.

source.rightsNote: The genuine passage comes from Shakespeare’s King John, first printed in the 1623 First Folio — centuries before 1931 and firmly in the public domain. (The modern idiom “gild the lily” itself is a common-usage phrase with no single copyrighted owner.)

author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright and poet, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. King John, a history play written in the mid-to-late 1590s, was first printed in the 1623 First Folio. Its line about gilding gold and painting the lily gave rise to a durable English idiom — in a form Shakespeare himself never used.

misattribution.heading: Why “gild the lily” isn’t Shakespeare
misattribution.intro: “Gilding the lily” is one of the most-quoted lines Shakespeare never wrote. It is a conflation of two images from a single sentence in King John.

items.why: Shakespeare’s Salisbury says it is excess “To gild refined gold, to paint the lily” — two distinct actions. Popular usage merged them, attaching “gild” to the “lily,” producing a phrase found nowhere in his text.
The underlying thought — that adding ornament to something already perfect is “wasteful and ridiculous excess” — is genuinely Shakespeare’s, from this same King John speech.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare wrote “paint the lily”; “gild the lily” is a later misquotation that overtook the original — as the Grammarphobia Blog and Wiktionary both document.

context.heading: How a mis-remembering became an idiom
lead: Salisbury’s speech in King John piles up images of pointless excess: gilding gold that is already refined, painting a lily that is already white, perfuming a violet. Each is a separate over-adornment. Somewhere in later retelling, the ‘gild’ of the gold jumped onto the ‘lily,’ and the two most vivid images fused into a single, punchier phrase.

The mongrel version won. “Gild the lily” is now standard English, printed by writers as careful as Edith Wharton, while Shakespeare’s actual “paint the lily” sounds almost wrong to modern ears — a rare case where the misquotation has all but replaced the original.
context.pull: He gilded the gold and painted the lily. Posterity gilded the lily.
